strengths: Identifies a novel and clean theoretical threshold (p >> dn) for full training-set reconstruction from a trained random features model, complementing and sharpening the classical p >> n threshold for label memorization/interpolation.

Rigorous, carefully executed proofs (Theorems 1 and 2) using non-trivial concentration and epsilon-net arguments, handling technical subtleties such as sign ambiguity tied to Hermite coefficient parity (Assumption 2, Remark 1).
Nice conceptual connection to prior work on the 'law of robustness' (p >> dn for smooth interpolation), suggesting a unifying link between adversarial robustness and data reconstructability.

Derives a concrete, efficiently implementable reconstruction algorithm (via projection residual minimization and conjugate gradient) directly motivated by the theory, and clearly explains its computational tricks.

Strong empirical validation across multiple settings: synthetic sphere data, CIFAR-10 binary and multi-class labels, and multiple architectures (random features, two-layer NN, deep ResNets), consistently confirming the predicted p ≈ dn transition.
Thoughtful ablation isolating the sign-ambiguity phenomenon predicted by theory (ReLU vs. ReLU+tanh), which strengthens the credibility of the theoretical mechanism.
Clear writing, good positioning relative to a broad and relevant related-work landscape (memorization, differential privacy, model inversion, dataset reconstruction attacks).
weaknesses: Theorem 2 (uniqueness/no-duplication of reconstructed samples) is only proven for n=2; the generalization to arbitrary n is asserted informally rather than rigorously established, leaving a gap between the theory and the general claim.

The theoretical results are confined to the random features model; extension to two-layer and deep residual networks is purely empirical with no formal justification, despite these being highlighted as key contributions.

The reconstruction algorithm assumes access to the exact trained parameter vector, network architecture, and (implicitly) the subspace structure in feature space—strong assumptions that may not hold for realistic memorization/privacy attack scenarios (e.g., LLMs), limiting real-world applicability.

No direct empirical comparison against existing dataset reconstruction baselines (e.g., Haim et al. 2022, Loo et al. 2024) on the same benchmarks, making it hard to gauge relative practical performance of the proposed method.

Experiments are conducted at fairly small scale (n on the order of 10-100, relatively small models), so it remains unclear how well the observed threshold and reconstruction quality extrapolate to larger, more realistic overparameterized regimes.

Key open problems (global optimality of the reconstruction loss, tractability of the non-convex optimization) are left unresolved, meaning the practical algorithm's success is only empirically observed rather than theoretically guaranteed, which somewhat undercuts the completeness of the 'law'.

Assumption 2's specific requirement on Hermite coefficient parity is fairly restrictive and excludes common activations like plain ReLU without modification, slightly limiting the generality of the clean-sign-recovery guarantee.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously proves a conceptually clean and novel threshold (p ≫ dn) for data reconstruction in the random features model, cleanly distinguishing it from the classical p ≫ n threshold for label interpolation/memorization—a genuine gap in the literature that prior work (Balle et al., Loo et al., Wang et al.) had not pinned down precisely.

The theoretical analysis is technically substantial, combining RF kernel concentration, Hermite decomposition, epsilon-net/uniform concentration arguments, and Stein-type lemmas; the proof sketches are reasonably clear and the appendix proofs appear carefully executed.

The paper derives a practical reconstruction algorithm directly motivated by the theory (minimizing the projection residual of θ* onto the reconstructed feature span), which is a nice bridge between theory and an implementable method.

Empirical validation is reasonably broad: synthetic sphere data, CIFAR-10 binary and multi-class labels, two-layer ReLU networks, and deep ResNets all show a consistent transition near p ≈ dn, lending credibility to the proposed law beyond the pure RF setting where theory applies.

The sign-ambiguity phenomenon for ReLU is explained theoretically (via Hermite parity) and then confirmed/resolved empirically with a mixed-parity activation, which is a nice consistency check between theory and experiment.
weaknesses: The flagship 'full dataset reconstruction' result (Theorem 2, ruling out duplicate/degenerate reconstructions) is only proved for n = 2; the paper offers no general-n argument or even a sketch of how the proof would scale, which significantly weakens the claim that 'the entire training dataset can be recovered' as stated in the abstract and title.

The theory is restricted to the random features model under fairly strong assumptions (sub-Gaussian data with fixed norm, Lipschitz activation with specific Hermite-coefficient parity conditions, n = O(d) regime); extension to two-layer and deep ResNet architectures is purely empirical with no theoretical backing, so the 'and Beyond' part of the title is not actually supported by analysis.

The reconstruction algorithm assumes complete white-box access to the trained parameters, the exact random feature matrix V, and the activation function—an idealized setting that is considerably stronger than realistic data-extraction threat models, limiting the practical/security significance of the 'law'.

Experiments are conducted at very small scale (n on the order of 10–100 samples, low-resolution 32×32 images, toy synthetic data) and do not include any comparison against existing reconstruction baselines (e.g., Haim et al. 2022, Buzaglo et al. 2023, Loo et al. 2024) on common ground, so it is unclear whether the proposed method/threshold offers any practical advantage over prior reconstruction attacks.

The actual over-parameterization requirement in Assumption 3 is p = ω(nd log^2 d), i.e., looser logarithmic factors are hidden in the 'dn' law; the empirical plots use thresholds at dn and 3dn without clearly reconciling this with the log-factor requirement, making the 'law' somewhat imprecise as stated.

No discussion of computational cost/scalability of the reconstruction optimization (conjugate gradient per step, Hungarian matching for evaluation) as n and d grow beyond the toy regimes tested, raising concerns about applicability to more realistic model/dataset sizes.

The paper's central practical implication (that reconstruction requires p ≫ dn, which is an extremely large parameter count relative to typical modern over-parameterized models) is only briefly discussed, and the significance/impact of the result for real privacy or copyright concerns in large models is left largely speculative.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously proves a novel over-parameterization threshold (p ≫ dn) for data reconstruction in random features models, complementing and sharply contrasting with the classical p ≫ n threshold for label interpolation. This fills an explicitly noted gap in the theoretical literature on memorization.

The theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) is technically sophisticated, combining Hermite decomposition, epsilon-net/uniform concentration arguments, and careful control of sub-Gaussian/sub-exponential random variables; proof sketches are clear and the full proofs in the appendix appear carefully executed.

The paper derives a concrete, practically implementable reconstruction algorithm directly motivated by the theory (minimizing the projection residual via gradient descent), and this algorithm is shown empirically to work well.

Strong empirical validation across multiple settings: synthetic data on the sphere, CIFAR-10 with binary and multi-class labels, and multiple architectures (RF, two-layer networks, and deep ResNets), consistently confirming the predicted p ≈ dn transition.

The authors are transparent about limitations and subtleties, e.g., the sign ambiguity for ReLU activations (explained via Hermite coefficient parity and experimentally confirmed/resolved), and they clearly delineate open problems (uniqueness of global optima, efficient optimization, intermediate regime n ≪ p ≪ dn).

Good situating of the work relative to prior theoretical work (Balle et al., Loo et al., Haim et al., Bubeck-Sellke law of robustness) and drawing an interesting connection between adversarial robustness thresholds and reconstruction thresholds.
Reasonable reproducibility: detailed implementation/optimization details and architecture specifications are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theorem 2, which rules out duplicate reconstructions and thus is needed to claim full dataset recovery, is only proven for n = 2; the general-n case is left open, so the strongest claim ("entire training set can be recovered") is not fully established theoretically beyond this special case.

The core theory assumes knowledge of the exact subspace span{φ(xi)}, while the practical algorithm only has access to θ* which lies in that subspace; the authors acknowledge (as an open problem) that there is no proof that minimizing the practical loss L(X̂) yields global optima corresponding to the true data, leaving a theory-practice gap.

Theoretical results are specific to the random features model; the extension to two-layer and deep residual networks is purely empirical without corresponding theoretical guarantees, despite these being highlighted as key experimental contributions.

The necessary activation assumption (existence of two non-zero Hermite coefficients of different parity beyond order 2) excludes the very common and practically important ReLU case for full sign recovery, and the fix of adding tanh to ReLU feels somewhat ad hoc rather than addressing the issue for the networks typically used in practice.

No direct quantitative comparison to existing reconstruction baselines (e.g., Haim et al. 2022, Buzaglo et al. 2023, Loo et al. 2024) in terms of reconstruction fidelity/metrics, making it hard to assess how the proposed method compares practically to prior attacks on the same data.

Experimental scale is fairly limited (small n, binary or few-class CIFAR-10 subsets, relatively simple ResNet variants without batch norm/pooling), which may limit insight into how the threshold behaves in more realistic, larger-scale settings.

The idealized data assumptions (fixed norm ∥x‖=√d, sub-Gaussianity) are standard in this line of theoretical work but somewhat distant from real image statistics, even though CIFAR-10 experiments partially mitigate this concern empirically.

strengths: Establishes a novel and precise theoretical threshold (p ≫ dn) for training-set reconstruction in the random features model, going beyond prior work that only handled the p→∞ regime (Loo et al.) or required strong assumptions (Balle et al., Wang et al.).

Rigorous, technically involved proofs (Theorems 1 and 2) using Hermite decomposition, ϵ-net concentration arguments, and careful control of higher-order terms; the proof sketches and appendix lemmas show a mature and self-contained analysis.
The theory directly motivates a concrete, computationally efficient reconstruction algorithm (projector-based loss solved via conjugate gradient, avoiding explicit matrix inversion).

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: synthetic sphere data, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, RF models, two-layer NNs, ResNets, and Vision Transformers, plus classification with logistic/cross-entropy losses — the p≈dn threshold appears remarkably consistently across all these settings even though the theory is only proven for RF regression.

Thoughtful discussion of edge cases (sign ambiguity from activation parity, Remark 1) that is both predicted theoretically and confirmed experimentally (Figures 4 and 10), demonstrating internal consistency between theory and practice.
Thorough ablation studies (learning rate sensitivity, mismatched number of reconstructed samples, weight decay, pruning) that strengthen confidence in the robustness of the phenomenon.

Clear positioning relative to related work (label memorization/interpolation literature, data reconstruction attacks, adversarial robustness laws) and an interesting connection drawn between the p≫dn threshold and prior robustness results.
Honest acknowledgment of open problems (extending Theorem 2 beyond n=2, proving global optimality of the practical loss, efficient optimization guarantees) rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Theorem 2, which rules out duplicate reconstructions, is only proven for n=2; the general-n case is left as a conjecture (Remark 2) supported only by empirical evidence, which is a significant theoretical gap given that practical applications require larger n.

There is a real gap between the theoretical guarantees (which assume access to the subspace span{φ(xi)} and characterize when a candidate set spans it) and the practical algorithm actually used in experiments (minimizing a non-convex loss purely from θ*); the paper does not prove that global optima of this practical objective correspond to correct reconstructions, only providing empirical support (Figure 2/9).

Assumption 2 on the activation function (zero 2nd Hermite coefficient, mixed-parity higher coefficients) technically excludes ReLU, the activation used in essentially all experiments; the theory-practice mismatch is handled only via the sign-ambiguity discussion, which is somewhat ad hoc.

The non-convex optimization used for reconstruction lacks convergence guarantees, and efficient solvability is explicitly left as an open problem, limiting the practical/theoretical completeness of the contribution.

Experiments are conducted on relatively small n (tens to ~100) and specific architectures/datasets; scalability of the reconstruction procedure to larger, more realistic settings (e.g., large language models, larger n) is not explored, limiting insight into real-world significance beyond the phenomenon being demonstrated.

The theory is restricted to random features models with i.i.d. Gaussian first layer, and while the paper shows the p≈dn threshold empirically extends to trained deep networks, there is no theoretical treatment for these more complex architectures, so the generalization claim rests entirely on empirical observation.

strengths: The paper provides a genuinely novel theoretical framing of memorization through the lens of data reconstruction (rather than label interpolation), identifying p ≫ dn as the key threshold -- a clean and intuitive generalization of the classical p ≫ n interpolation threshold.

Theorem 1 is a rigorous, non-trivial result proved via careful high-dimensional probability tools (ε-net arguments, Hermite decompositions, Bernstein-type concentration), and the proof sketches are clearly communicated.

The empirical validation is extensive and consistent: synthetic data, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, across random features, two-layer networks, ResNets, and vision transformers, with multiple loss functions (square, logistic, cross-entropy). The qualitative threshold behavior (p≈n for fitting, p≈dn for reconstruction) replicates robustly across all these settings.

Thoughtful ablations (learning rate sensitivity, reconstructing with incorrect nhat, weight decay, pruning) strengthen confidence that the phenomenon is not an artifact of a specific experimental choice.

The sign-ambiguity analysis (Remark 1) tied to Hermite coefficient parity is a nice theoretical prediction that is explicitly confirmed/falsified in controlled experiments (ReLU vs. ReLU+tanh), showing good alignment between theory and practice.
weaknesses: The central claim that the 'entire training dataset' can be reconstructed is only rigorously established for n=2 (Theorem 2); for general n the absence-of-duplicates argument is left as a conjecture (Remark 2), so the paper's titular 'law' is not fully proven as stated for general n, only strongly suggested by theory + experiments.

There is a non-trivial gap between what the theory proves (sufficiency conditions on span inclusion given an oracle Xˆ) and the actual algorithm used in practice (minimizing L(Xˆ) via gradient descent from random initialization). The paper acknowledges this gap as an 'open problem' (global optimality of L and tractability of its non-convex optimization), meaning the practical procedure's success is only empirically, not theoretically, justified.

The extension to two-layer networks, ResNets, and ViTs is purely empirical/heuristic -- there is no theoretical argument (even informal) for why the RF-derived threshold p ≫ dn (in terms of last-layer width) should transfer to these architectures with trained intermediate layers, feature learning, and non-Gaussian representations.

Activation assumptions (Assumption 2, e.g., specific non-zero Hermite coefficients of mixed parity for order ≥3) are fairly restrictive and exclude common activations like pure ReLU for full sign recovery, which is only patched with an ad hoc ReLU+tanh activation in experiments rather than addressed by extending the theory.

No empirical comparison against existing reconstruction baselines (e.g., Haim et al.'s KKT-based method, Loo et al.'s NTK-based approach) is provided, despite these being discussed as closely related in the text; this makes it hard to judge whether the proposed method/threshold offers practical advantages over prior reconstruction attacks.

Experimental scale remains modest (n in the tens to low hundreds, moderate d), and the method requires knowledge of n (or searching over nˆ) and of model internals (V, φ, all layer weights) -- a strong 'white-box' assumption whose practical relevance to real privacy/memorization concerns (e.g., in LLMs) is not demonstrated.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously proves a novel over-parameterization threshold (p ≫ dn) for data reconstruction, clearly distinguishing it from the classical p ≫ n threshold for label interpolation — a conceptually clean and significant theoretical contribution.

The theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) is technically careful, using sophisticated high-dimensional probability tools (Hermite decompositions, epsilon-net arguments, Bernstein-type concentration, generalized Stein's lemma) and is presented with clear proof sketches plus full, detailed proofs in the appendix.
The theory directly motivates a practical, principled reconstruction algorithm (minimizing the projection residual loss), bridging theory and an applicable method.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: synthetic spherical data, CIFAR-10, Tiny-ImageNet, random features, two-layer networks, deep ResNets, and vision transformers, all showing consistent transitions at p ≈ dn.

Thorough ablation studies (step size sensitivity, mismatched number of reconstructed samples, weight decay/ridge regularization, network pruning), which strengthen confidence in the robustness of the phenomenon.
Nice auxiliary theoretical insight (Remark 1) connecting Hermite coefficient parity to sign ambiguity in reconstruction, which is explicitly confirmed by targeted experiments (ReLU vs. ReLU+tanh).

Honest discussion of limitations and clearly stated open problems (e.g., general n in Theorem 2, global optimality of the reconstruction loss, regime n ≪ p ≪ dn), which situates the contribution appropriately within the broader literature on memorization and privacy.
weaknesses: Theorem 2 (ruling out duplicate reconstructions) is only proven for n = 2; the generalization to arbitrary n is left as a conjecture/future work (Remark 2), somewhat limiting the completeness of the main theoretical result.

The core theoretical guarantee assumes knowledge of the subspace spanned by training features, while the actual algorithm operates on a different, weaker-looking objective (projecting θ*); the gap between these is only validated empirically (Figure 2), not proven.

No theoretical guarantee that gradient descent on the proposed non-convex reconstruction loss finds a good solution, nor that all global optima correspond to true reconstructions — both left as open problems.

The neural network extensions (two-layer, ResNet, ViT) are purely empirical, with no theoretical backing beyond the RF case, so the generality of the "law" to deep architectures remains a conjecture based on simulations with fairly small n.

Activation function assumptions are somewhat restrictive (need mixed-parity Hermite coefficients for sign identifiability), and standard activations like ReLU only partially satisfy them, leading to a known failure mode (sign-flip) that the main theory does not cover.

No direct quantitative comparison against existing reconstruction baselines (e.g., Haim et al. 2022, Loo et al. 2024) in terms of reconstruction quality or required over-parameterization, which would help contextualize the practical significance of the identified threshold.
